title: Diagnostic performance of aortic valve calcium and CT-derived aortic valve area in low-gradient aortic stenosis.
authors: Dakota De Cecco; Christopher Scoma; Corey Powell; Megan Joseph; William Truesdell; Stanley Chetcuti; Andrew W Harris
abstract:
Practice guidelines recommend the use of computed tomography (CT) aortic valve calcium (AVC) scores for patients with low-gradient aortic stenosis (LG-AS). AVC has not been studied in comparison to invasive aortic valve study (IAVS).
To determine the diagnostic performance of AVC and CT-derived aortic valve area (CT-AVA) compared to IAVS as a reference standard.
We included consecutive patients with LG-AS with echocardiography, CT and IAVS performed within 1 year at a single tertiary center. Severe AS was defined by aortic valve area (AVA) ≤1.0 cm2 measured by IAVS. CT-AVA was retrospectively measured by a blinded reader. CT-AVA and sex-based AVC were compared to AS defined by IAVS. Diagnostic performance was compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. AVC and CT-AVA were compared to cardiac events consisting of death, aortic valve replacement and cardiovascular hospitalization.
Out of 294 patients in the overall cohort, 206 patients with definite AS severity by IAVS were included as the primary diagnostic cohort. Severe AS according to invasive AVA (≤1.0 cm2) was present in 72 patients (35.0%). Sex-based AVC scores had relatively poor diagnostic performance compared to the reference IAVS with AUCs of 0.59 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48-0.70) and 0.58 (95% CI 0.45-0.71) for men and women, respectively. CT-AVA had better diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.77-0.87).
In our study population, CT-AVA had significantly better diagnostic performance than AVC compared to the reference standard, IAVS.

title: In-Hospital Mortality After Aortic Valve Replacement Surgical Versus Transcatheter: A Nationwide Study with Machine Learning-Based Risk Prediction.
authors: Akash Sharma; Mohamed Jamshid Ubaid; Fnu Shalini; Hamza Yousaf
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are two preferred methods for treating aortic stenosis. This study compared the in-hospital mortality rates associated with SAVR and TAVR.
In accordance with the STROBE guidelines, we conducted an analytical cross-sectional study utilizing data from the National Readmission Database (NRD) spanning from 2016 to 2020. Patients who underwent TAVR or SAVR were identified using specific ICD-10 procedure codes. We employed adjusted multivariate logistic regression analysis to determine the odds ratio (OR) of death associated with SAVR compared to TAVR. Patients were followed for a year and OR with 95% CI were calculated. AI based XGBoost model were used to find the predictors of mortality.
Our study included a total of 361,875 patients. Among these, 182,443 underwent TAVR, while 179,432 underwent SAVR. In the TAVR group, 2,563 patients (1.4%) died during hospitalization, whereas 6,671 patients (3.7%) died in the SAVR group. The multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that SAVR is associated with higher in-hospital mortality (OR = 2.66, 95% CI 2.51-2.81, p < 0.001) compared to TAVR. Follow up data at 30 days, three months, six months, did not find any difference in mortality between TAVR and SAVR. Notably, liver failure, HLD, renal failure, SAVR, female, CHF, and atrial fibrillation are amongst the top predictor of mortality in patients undergoing (TAVR or SAVR). While in cardiac rehospitalization, risk factors like female gender, CHF, Afib, HLD, DM have higher predictability than procedure.
Our study demonstrates that SAVR is associated with a higher likelihood of in-hospital mortality compared to TAVR, with organ dysfunction (liver failure, kidney dysfunction) as a predictor of mortality.

title: Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation in Dextrocardia: Lessons From a Complex Redo Case.
authors: Jun Fu; Zhixiang Gu; Jinpeng Li; Dongsi Shuang; Bao Sun; Yiliyasi Yimingjiang; Lin Chen
journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
abstract: Dextrocardia with situs solitus poses significant surgical challenges for left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation, particularly in patients with prior sternotomy and complex valvular disease. We report on a 60 year old man with dextrocardia, advanced heart failure, prior mechanical mitral valve replacement, and bicuspid aortic valve disease who underwent successful Corheart 6 LVAD implantation during redo sternotomy with concomitant bioprosthetic aortic and mitral valve replacement. Intraoperative findings included extensive pannus/thrombus on the mechanical mitral prosthesis (causing relative stenosis) and an unsuspected 10 g left atrial thrombus, both of which were removed. Total cardiopulmonary bypass time was 330 minutes, and aortic cross‑clamp time was 233 minutes. Postoperative acute kidney injury requiring dialysis resolved, and the patient was discharged after 137 days. At 1 year follow-up, the left ventricular end-diastolic diameter decreased from 69 to 66 mm, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) remained stable (28-25%), New York Heart Association (NYHA) class improved from IIIb‑IV to II, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) recovered from 32 ml/min at 9 months to 51 ml/min at 1 year.

title: Integrating volumes into myocardial work: the prognostic role of non-invasive pressure-strain-volume analysis in transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
authors: Tímea K Turschl; Zsuzsanna Ladányi; Andrea Ferencz; Alexandra Fábián; Márton Tokodi; Ádám Szijártó; Mihály Ruppert; Andrea Nagy; Andrea Á Molnár; Levente Molnár; Endre Zima; Attila Kovács; Bálint K Lakatos; Béla Merkely
abstract: The accurate echocardiographic assessment of the left ventricular (LV) contractile state remains challenging in aortic stenosis, as ejection fraction and even global longitudinal strain are markedly load-dependent. The novel pressure-strain loop-derived myocardial work were developed to overcome this limitation; however, incorporation of instantaneous LV volume may further improve this method. We aimed to quantify myocardial work using pressure-strain-volume (PSV) loops and to evaluate its prognostic value in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). We enrolled 300 patients scheduled for TAVI (age 78.7 ± 6.3 years, 41% female). The endpoint was all-cause mortality, reached by 62 patients over a median follow-up of 25 months. Echocardiography and non-invasive blood pressure measurements were performed one day before TAVI. LV pressure was estimated noninvasively, while strain curves were derived from speckle-tracking analysis. Pressure-strain relations were adjusted to instantaneous LV volumes to construct PSV loops, yielding volume-adjusted indices (GWIVi and GCWVi). GWIVi showed similar extent of LV dysfunction in classical and paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS phenotypes compared to the normal flow-high gradient patients (46.98 ± 20.71 vs. 51.99 ± 18.43 vs. 63.74 ± 22.26 mmHg%L/m2, p < 0.001), while other LV function parameters did not. In multivariable Cox-regression, GWIVi was an independent predictor of mortality (Hazard ratio: 0.955 [confidence interval: 0.773-0.993], p < 0.05) alongside clinically relevant other markers such as hemoglobin and atrial fibrillation. PSV loop-derived myocardial work detected LV mechanical differences between AS phenotypes and provided independent prognostic value in TAVI candidates, potentially offering a more physiologically accurate assessment of LV function in this population.

title: Carotid atherosclerosis and aortic stiffness in masters athletes: Multimodality vascular phenotyping from the Master@Heart study.
authors: Rik Pauwels; Christophe Dausin; Ruben De Bosscher; Jarne De Paepe; Youri Bekhuis; Boris Delpire; Kasper Favere; Jürgen Duchenne; Thijs M H Eijsvogels; Peter Sinnaeve; Steven Dymarkowski; Olivier Ghekiere; Tatiana Kuznetsova; Caroline M Van De Heyning; Paul L Van Herck; Tomas Robyns; Lieven Herbots; André La Gerche; Hein Heidbuchel; Rik Willems; Guido Claessen
abstract:
Middle-aged male Masters athletes exhibit a higher burden of coronary atherosclerosis on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) compared with healthy controls. Whether this is accompanied by differences in carotid atherosclerosis or aortic stiffness remains uncertain. We assessed carotid atherosclerosis and aortic stiffness across groups, association between carotid atherosclerosis and coronary disease, and the incremental value of carotid plaque beyond traditional risk factors.
In this cross-sectional analysis of the Master@Heart study, 549 low cardiovascular risk men (median age 55 [50-60] years), including lifelong athletes, late-onset athletes, and healthy controls, underwent vascular phenotyping. Carotid plaque was assessed by ultrasound, aortic stiffness by carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (PWV), and coronary atherosclerosis by CCTA. Group differences were assessed using chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Association between carotid and coronary atherosclerosis was evaluated using regression models. Incremental discriminatory value was assessed using ROC curve analysis.
Prevalence of ≥1 carotid plaque did not differ between lifelong athletes, late-onset athletes, and controls (29.5%vs. 33.2% vs. 27.9%; p = 0.54). Carotid stenosis ≥50% was rare (1.2%-2.7%) and similar across groups (p = 0.54). Median PWV did not differ between groups (p = 0.29). Carotid plaque was associated with coronary atherosclerosis on CCTA. However, adding carotid plaque to traditional risk factors did not improve discrimination of coronary atherosclerosis.
In middle-aged male Masters athletes, excess subclinical coronary atherosclerosis is observed without corresponding differences in carotid plaque or aortic stiffness. Although carotid plaque is associated with coronary atherosclerosis, it does not meaningfully improve risk discrimination beyond traditional risk factors.

title: Arterial tortuosity syndrome with coronary artery involvement in a middle-aged female: A case report.
authors: Prinsa Shrestha; Amin Shah; Saroj Gc; Niraj Kumar Sharma; Aditya Mahaseth; Sanjaya Kumar Shrestha
abstract: Arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) is a rare autosomal recessive connective-tissue arteriopathy characterized by diffuse elongation and tortuosity of large and medium-sized arteries. Although it is typically diagnosed during childhood, adult presentation may occur and can be overlooked when overt connective-tissue manifestations are absent; coronary involvement is uncommon but clinically important. A 41-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of exertional substernal chest pain and dyspnea. CT coronary angiography demonstrated marked tortuosity of the left main coronary artery with focal kinking approximately 6.8 mm from its origin and 40-45% luminal stenosis (CAD-RADS 2). Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated generalized arterial elongation and marked tortuosity involving the thoracic aorta, supra-aortic branches, and abdominal aortic branches, together with early branching of the main pulmonary artery, without aneurysm, dissection, or intramural hematoma. Conventional coronary angiography was technically unsuccessful because of severe arterial tortuosity, with unsuccessful catheter advancement and coronary engagement despite radial and subsequent femoral access. The overall clinical and imaging findings were highly suggestive of ATS with coronary involvement, although molecular genetic confirmation was not available. The patient was managed conservatively with vascular risk-factor optimization and structured follow-up, with symptomatic improvement at one month. This case highlights that ATS may present in adulthood with coronary artery tortuosity and focal kinking and emphasizes the importance of recognizing diffuse multi-territory arterial tortuosity on CT. Comprehensive vascular imaging can establish a strong radiological suspicion of ATS, identify coronary involvement and procedural challenges, and guide surveillance even when genetic confirmation is unavailable.

title: Rapid Progression of Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy With Sudden Cardiac Death Within the First Year of Heart Transplantation: A Case Report.
authors: Malcom Dix; Jean-Pierre Iskandar; Lefan He; Mohaned S Serdah; Aditya A Joshi; Anuradha Godishala; Abhishek Chaturvedi; Katherine Kaproth-Joslin; David A Dombroski; YeeAnn Chen; Wendy A Cheruiyot; Ronald Chong-Yik; Ronald G Schwartz; Jeffrey Alexis; Igor Gosev; Katherine L Wood; Sabu Thomas
abstract: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is a major cause of mortality and morbidity within the first 3 years of heart transplantation (HT). CAV results in progressive coronary artery stenosis and may lead to arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. In some cases, sudden cardiac death represents the initial presentation of CAV, as cardiac denervation blunts anginal symptoms that otherwise could have preceded sudden cardiac death (SCD). Here, we describe the case of a 56-year-old man with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. He underwent left ventricular assist device implantation followed by orthotopic HT. Five months after transplantation, he presented with atypical mid-sternal chest discomfort initially thought to be musculoskeletal in origin. Routine coronary angiography at 12 months revealed severe, diffuse 3-vessel disease consistent with International Society of Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) CAV-3, and cardiac MRI revealed full thickness delayed enhancement in the inferior wall consistent with infarction. Despite overall preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, he developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) with an appropriate shock from a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) and was transferred with an intra-aortic balloon pump to a larger transplant center and underwent another heart transplantation. This case highlights rapid CAV progression leading to infarction and arrhythmia despite preserved LVEF, emphasizing the need for enhanced screening with biomarkers and imaging as well as earlier consideration for device-based strategies to prevent sudden cardiac death in high-risk transplant recipients.

title: Achieving Reliable Peripheral Nerve Blockade in Cardiogenic Shock With Distorted Femoral Anatomy: A Case Report.
authors: Mohammed I Hakami; Ayman H Mustafa
abstract: Patients with cardiogenic shock and severe structural heart disease may poorly tolerate both general and neuraxial anesthesia. In selected cases, peripheral nerve blockade may reduce hemodynamic disturbance, but the block must be reliable when pain, sympathetic stimulation, or emergency conversion to general anesthesia could be poorly tolerated. We report a 62-year-old woman with cardiogenic shock, low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis, advanced dilated cardiomyopathy, pulmonary edema, orthopnea, and active femoral bleeding who required urgent femoral artery and vein repair. General anesthesia and neuraxial anesthesia were considered hazardous. Hematoma and anasarca distorted the femoral anatomy and prevented direct femoral nerve visualization. Combined ultrasound guidance and nerve stimulation were used to support safe needle advancement and functional nerve localization. Surgery proceeded with minimal sedation and without escalation of vasoactive support. This case highlights the role of reliability-focused peripheral nerve blockade when conventional anesthetic options are high risk and regional anatomy is distorted.

title: Construction and implantation of a modified trileaflet polytetrafluoroethylene valved conduit for pulmonary valve replacement.
authors: Abel Getachew; Nikita Zadneulitca; Ashok Muralidaran; Castigliano M Bhamidipati; Yoshio Ootaki
abstract:
Handmade expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) valved conduits have emerged as a durable and cost-effective option for pulmonary valve replacement. We have reported excellent results of trileaflet ePTFE valved conduit and the longest follow-up exceeded 10 years. Technical precision during valve construction and implantation is critical to optimize valve function and conduit geometry, and we recently modified the technique. We report our updated technique and clinical outcomes.
The conduit was constructed intraoperatively on a sterile back table while the patient was being prepared by the anesthesia team. Leaflet dimensions were calculated based on conduit diameter, and leaflets were fashioned with 1 mm extensions at each end to reinforce commissural attachment, then sutured to an ePTFE tube graft using 3 CV-5 sutures with external knot tying. The graft was rotated during construction to ensure accurate leaflet alignment and valve competence was confirmed prior to implantation. During implantation, the main pulmonary artery was divided to optimize conduit geometry, minimizing the posterior conduit length and the graft trimmed in a trapezoidal fashion to reduce tension and improve alignment.
Fifty-four patients received ePTFE valved conduit. Conduit sizes were 18 mm (n = 7), 20 mm (n = 9), 22 mm (n = 1), 24 mm (n = 36), and 28 mm (n = 1). Median follow-up was 1.4 years (maximum, 4.3 years). There was 1 mortality during follow-up due to infectious pseudoaneurysm of the aortic root after Ross procedure. One patient developed severe pulmonary insufficiency after surgery. Recent echocardiography showed no significant pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary insufficiency, or valve deterioration in the remaining patients, and no catheter-based or surgical reinterventions have been required to date.
This refined technique for the construction and implantation of a trileaflet ePTFE valved conduit is simple, reproducible, and yields excellent early hemodynamic results. Attention to leaflet design, commissural security, and conduit geometry may contribute to low early failure rates and favorable valve performance. Longer-term follow-up is ongoing to assess durability.

title: Prenatal diagnosis of mitral-pulmonary intervalvular fibrosa pseudoaneurysm associated with TGA causing severe pulmonary stenosis: A rare case report.
authors: Aliya Kemal Ahsan; Putri Yubbu; Anizah Aishah Rosli
abstract:
Pseudoaneurysm of the mitral-aortic intervalvular fibrosa is a rare and typically acquired cardiac lesion, with congenital forms being exceptionally uncommon, particularly when identified prenatally. We report the case of a 23-year-old gravida 2 woman with one previous history of miscarriage who was referred at 25 weeks' gestation for a fetal intracardiac mass. Fetal echocardiography revealed a cystic echogenic mass at the crux of the heart, consistent with a pseudoaneurysm arising from the mitral-pulmonary intervalvular fibrosa (MPIVF) associated with transposition of the great arteries, causing severe left ventricular outflow tract obstruction or subvalvular pulmonary stenosis. The cardiac lesion was also associated with a large mid-muscular ventricular septal defect alongside a small left ventricle suggestive of single-ventricle physiology. This constellation of findings pointed to a diagnosis of complex cyanotic congenital heart disease with possible ductal-dependent pulmonary circulation. Prenatal diagnosis enabled early parental counseling, planning for delivery at a tertiary cardiac center, and postnatal preparation for prostaglandin therapy and surgical evaluation. This case highlights the importance of recognizing MPIVF pseudoaneurysm in the fetal period, particularly when associated with obstructive physiology or major structural anomalies, and contributes to the limited literature on congenital variants of this condition.
Pseudoaneurysm of the mitral-pulmonary intervalvular fibrosa is an exceptionally rare congenital lesion. Its association with transposition of the great arteries, ventricular septal defect, and left ventricular outflow tract obstruction has important prognostic and surgical implications. Prenatal echocardiography is key for recognition, particularly when there is a cystic or echogenic intracardiac mass with a to-and-fro Doppler flow near the atrioventricular junction. Prenatal echocardiography is crucial for early counseling and planned delivery at a tertiary cardiac center.

title: Low-dose juglone attenuates pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy through Lys207-dependent FoxO1 activation and mitochondrial protection.
authors: Hongyu Chen; Zhihao Yang; Cheng Zhang; Chengxin Ge; Yingliang Zhao; Shaopeng Cheng; Yilin Wang; Hao Chen; Can Xu; Dongjin Wang; Jie Yang
abstract: Pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance. Here, we investigated the efficacy, safety window, and redox-regulatory mechanism of juglone, a naturally occurring 5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone. In mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction (TAC), high-dose juglone induced cardiac, hepatic, and renal toxicity, whereas 1 mg/kg/day was well tolerated and attenuated cardiac hypertrophy. Juglone also suppressed Ang II-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro and preserved mitochondrial ultrastructure and mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration, ATP production, and redox homeostasis. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that juglone reduced stress-associated cardiomyocyte states and enriched calcium-handling cardiomyocytes. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, Biotin-Juglone pull-down assay, surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assays, molecular docking, and mutational analyses identified FoxO1 as a functional target of juglone. Juglone engaged the FoxO1 DNA-binding domain in a Lys207-dependent manner, and was associated with FoxO1 deacetylation, nuclear accumulation, and transcriptional activation. Activated FoxO1 induced Sesn3 transcription and restored AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172. Sesn3 silencing markedly attenuated juglone-induced AMPK activation and impaired its protective effects against cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. FoxO1 silencing, FoxO1-K207Q mutation, blockade of FoxO1 deacetylation, or inhibition of FoxO1 transcriptional activity impaired these benefits. Importantly, myocardium from patients with aortic valve stenosis-associated hypertrophy exhibited increased FoxO1 acetylation, reduced cardiomyocyte nuclear FoxO1 localization, decreased Sesn3 expression and AMPK phosphorylation, and increased 4-HNE. Collectively, low-dose juglone attenuates pathological hypertrophy and preserves mitochondrial homeostasis through the FoxO1-Sesn3-AMPK axis, while highlighting the importance of dose-dependent redox effects in determining its therapeutic efficacy and systemic toxicity.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment and cardiovascular outcomes following aortic valve replacement: a nationwide observational study.
authors: Lytfi Krasniqi; Mohanad Hamandi; Poul Erik Mortensen; Henrik Nissen; Patricia A Pellikka; Barry A Borlaug; Oke Gerke; Amal Haujir; Louise Oeksnebjerg Krasniqi; Christian Juhl Terkelsen; Lars Peter Riber; Jordi Sanchez Dahl
abstract:
GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce major adverse cardiovascular events among patients with diabetes, overweight, and obesity. Whether these benefits extend to patients undergoing aortic valve replacement (AVR) for severe aortic stenosis (AS) remains unknown. Thus, we investigated the association between GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment and cardiovascular outcomes after AVR.
Nationwide population-based cohort study including consecutive patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI or SAVR in Western Denmark between January, 2016 and April, 2022. Patients were followed until death, emigration, crossover, or end of follow up on May 12, 2026. Propensity score-matching was performed to balance confounding. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, or aortic valve reoperation. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, aortic valve reoperation, with analyses accounting for the competing risk of death.
Among 5259 eligible patients undergoing AVR, 292 propensity score-matched patients were included in the final analyses. During a mean follow up of 4.8±2.4 years, GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment was associated with a lower risk of the primary composite outcome compared with controls (HR 0.69, 95%CI 0.50-0.96, p=0.029). GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment was also associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality (HR 0.66, 95%CI 0.46-0.95, p=0.025). In competing risk analyses accounting for death, lower risks were observed for heart failure hospitalization (HR 0.67, 95%CI 0.48-0.93, p=0.018), and aortic valve reoperation (HR 0.69, 95%CI 0.49-0.98, p=0.037).
Treatment with GLP-1 receptor agonists was associated with lower risk of cardiovascular outcomes including mortality following AVR among patients with severe AS.

title: Perioperative B-Cell-Targeted Therapy for High-Risk Valve Surgery in Active Primary Sjögren's Disease.
authors: Bing Li; Lili Pan; Hua Liao
abstract:
Primary Sjögren's disease (SjD) is a systemic autoimmune disease driven by B-cell dysregulation. Clinically significant valvular involvement is uncommon, and evidence guiding perioperative immunomodulation remains limited.
A 59-year-old woman with SjD and severe aortic stenosis required valve replacement. Preoperative evaluation demonstrated active SjD with elevated inflammatory markers and hypergammaglobulinemia. Following multidisciplinary discussion, telitacicept, corticosteroids, and hydroxychloroquine were initiated before surgery. After improvement in inflammatory activity, the patient underwent aortic valve and ascending aorta replacement. Histopathologic examination showed degenerative valvular changes with focal inflammatory cell infiltration. The postoperative course was uneventful, with normal prosthetic valve function at 1-year follow-up.
This case highlights the challenges of managing severe valvular heart disease in patients with active primary SjD and a multidisciplinary perioperative strategy incorporating B-cell-targeted therapy. Although preoperative immunomodulation may have attenuated the histopathologic evidence of immune-mediated valvular involvement, the case offers insights when guidance is limited.

title: Intraoperative ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Complicating Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair.
authors: Xunlai Lu; Yuanjia Luo; Fanjing Wang; Wei Cao; Jing Cheng; Peng Lu; Shenrui Xu; Jiachao Luo
abstract:
Acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction concurrent with endovascular aneurysm repair for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is an extremely rare and life-threatening emergency, currently lacking unified clinical guidelines for reference.
A 61-year-old male patient underwent endovascular aneurysm repair for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm and experienced persistent hypotension during the procedure. Postprocedural electrocardiogram and cardiac enzyme tests confirmed acute ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. The patient underwent emergency coronary angiography, which revealed severe stenosis, followed by successful balloon angioplasty. The patient recovered and was discharged following multidisciplinary postoperative care.
This case demonstrates the management principles for multiple life-threatening complications, where the clinical challenge formed by the huge retroperitoneal hematoma (bleeding risk) and the requirement for antiplatelet therapy after urgent revascularization (ischemic risk) was properly addressed. Through accurate identification, precise intervention, and multidisciplinary team collaboration, the patient was successfully rescued. This case provides a referable practical path for clinical decision-making in similar rare scenarios, highlighting the critical value of individualized treatment strategies.

title: Dapagliflozin After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation According to Frailty in DapaTAVI Trial.
authors: Rafael Gonzalez-Manzanares; Soledad Ojeda; Ignacio Amat-Santos; Albert Ariza-Solé; Rafael Romaguera; Diego López Otero; Luis Nombela-Franco; Livia Gheorge; Jorge Sanz-Sánchez; Carlos Baladrón Zorita; Ignacio Gallo; Rafael Cobas Paz; Antonio Jesús Muñoz García; Victoria Vilalta; Gabriela Veiga Fernández; Juan Gabriel Córdoba Soriano; Pedro Cepas-Gillén; Miriam Sandín Rollán; Xacobe Flores Ríos; Ricardo Palma-Carbajal; Roberto Martín Reyes; Pablo Avanzas; Sergio García Blas; Juan A Franco-Peláez; Javier Martín Moreiras; José Ramón Gonzalez Juanatey; Nieves Gonzalo; German Calle; José Luis Díez; Sandra Santos-Martínez; Rocío González Ferreiro; Erika Muñoz García; Eduard Fernandez-Nofrerias; Xoan Sanmartín; Gabriela Tirado; Alejandro Gutierrez Barri; Inmaculada González Bermúdez; Xavier Rosselló; Valentín Fuster; Borja Ibáñez; Sergio Raposeiras Roubín
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
abstract:
Frailty is common in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation and portends worse outcomes. Whether the benefit of posttranscatheter aortic valve implantation dapagliflozin differs by frailty is uncertain.
In this post hoc analysis, we investigated the efficacy of dapagliflozin according to frailty status in the DapaTAVI (Dapagliflozin in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation) trial. Frailty was assessed through the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illnesses, and Loss of Weight scale (robust=0, prefrail=1-2, frail=3-5). The primary outcome was the composite of all-cause death or worsening heart failure at 1 year.
Among 1222 patients with baseline frailty assessment, 47.2% were frail, 40.3% prefrail, and 12.4% robust. Over 12 months, 215 patients (17.6%) experienced the primary end point. Patients who were prefrail and frail had higher risk than robust patients (adjusted hazard ratios [HRs], 1.88 [95% CI, 1.05-3.38] and 2.29 [1.29-4.07], respectively; P=0.004). Dapagliflozin was associated with a lower risk of the primary end point in patients who were frail (HR, 0.53 [95% CI, 0.36-0.77]) but not in those who were prefrail (HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.66-1.55]) or robust patients (HR, 1.26 [95% CI, 0.42-3.75]); P for interaction=0.021. There was no evidence that frailty modified the safety profile of dapagliflozin.
Frailty was common and independently associated with worse outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Dapagliflozin appeared to confer greater relative benefit in patients with frailty.

title: Impact of prolonged balloon inflation on valve expansion and early clinical outcomes following contemporary balloon-expandable transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
authors: Francesco Cardaioli; Luca Nai Fovino; Tommaso Fabris; Giulia Masiero; Andrea Panza; Massimo Napodano; Chiara Fraccaro; Francesco Putortì; Giuseppe Tarantini
journal: EuroIntervention : journal of EuroPCR in collaboration with the Working Group on Interventional Cardiology of the European Society of Cardiology
abstract:
Incomplete expansion of balloon-expandable (BE) transcatheter heart valves (THVs) after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) may affect valve performance and durability. Routine THV post-dilatation (the "double-tap" technique) has been proposed to optimise device expansion; however, it may increase procedural complexity.
We sought to evaluate the impact of a prolonged balloon inflation implantation strategy on BE THV expansion, haemodynamic performance, and early clinical outcomes.
This single-centre study analysed consecutive TAVI patients treated for native tricuspid aortic stenosis with the SAPIEN 3 Ultra RESILIA THV using a prolonged balloon inflation strategy (8 seconds). Valve expansion was assessed by fluoroscopy at multiple frame levels and compared with three validated reference standards. Results were also descriptively compared with previously published data on the double-tap technique. Clinical and haemodynamic outcomes at 30 days were adjudicated according to Valve Academic Research Consortium 3 criteria.
A total of 84 patients (mean age 78.8 years, 58% male, median Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality score 3.9%) were included. Prolonged inflation resulted in complete THV expansion at the inflow and outflow levels, with only mild underexpansion (98.5±1.3%) detected at the midframe level when manufacturer-defined nominal values were used as the reference. When compared with previously published data on the double-tap technique, expansion values for the 23, 26, and 29 mm valves were consistently similar or higher, whereas lower expansion was observed for the 20 mm size. Device success was achieved in all cases, with no stroke at 30 days. Permanent pacemaker implantation occurred in 6% of patients. Haemodynamic performance was favourable (mean gradient 9.2 [interquartile range 7.0-10.3] mmHg at 30 days), with no patients having moderate or severe paravalvular leak.
Prolonged balloon inflation during BE THV deployment is associated with favourable valve expansion, haemodynamic results, and a favourable safety profile, consistent with values reported in double-tap series. If confirmed in larger studies, this strategy may represent a simple alternative to routine double-tap in selected patients.

title: Tracking Active Fibroblast-Mediated Tissue Remodelling in Cardiomyopathies: Translational Insights from FAPI PET Imaging.
authors: Inês Fortuna; Janete Santos; Paula Soeiro; Raquel Machado; Ana Oliveira; Jorge Pereira; Giuseppe Limongelli; Teresa Faria; Elisabete Martins; European Reference Network for Rare, Low-Prevalence, or Complex Diseases of the Heart (ERN GUARD-Heart)
abstract: Myocardial fibrosis is a major pathological component of cardiac remodelling and contributes to ventricular stiffness, impaired myocardial function, heart failure progression, and arrhythmic vulnerability across a broad spectrum of cardiomyopathies. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), fibrotic remodelling encompasses both diffuse interstitial matrix expansion and focal replacement fibrosis and is closely associated with disease severity and adverse clinical outcomes. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), using late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and quantitative parametric mapping, is central to non-invasive myocardial tissue characterization. LGE primarily identifies focal areas of replacement fibrosis and scar, whereas native T1, T2, and extracellular volume (ECV) mapping provide complementary information on diffuse myocardial and interstitial tissue abnormalities, including extracellular matrix expansion. However, these techniques characterize the structural and tissue-level consequences of myocardial injury and remodelling rather than directly visualizing the cellular processes underlying fibroblast activation. Fibroblast activation protein inhibitor positron emission tomography (FAPI PET) has emerged as a promising molecular imaging approach for assessing active fibroblast-mediated tissue remodelling. By targeting fibroblast activation protein (FAP), a cell-surface serine protease upregulated in activated fibroblasts and myofibroblasts. FAPI radiotracers may provide a molecular readout of accessible FAP expression that complements structural and tissue characterization by CMR. This review examines the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying active myocardial remodelling, with particular emphasis on transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)/Smad signalling, fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition, FAP expression, and extracellular matrix turnover. We critically evaluate the current clinical evidence for FAPI PET/CT and hybrid PET/CMR across cardiomyopathies, focusing on HCM while also considering ischemic, inflammatory, infiltrative, and other non-ischemic forms of cardiac remodelling. Particular attention is given to the relationship between myocardial FAPI uptake, CMR tissue characterization, ventricular function, circulating biomarkers, and calculated arrhythmic risk. Although initial studies support the complementary value of FAPI PET and CMR for characterizing active and established myocardial remodelling, the available evidence remains limited by small, predominantly single-centre cohorts, heterogeneous radiotracers and acquisition protocols, and the absence of validated quantitative thresholds or prospective outcome data. Larger longitudinal studies are required to determine whether FAPI PET can provide incremental prognostic information or serve as a reproducible imaging biomarker for disease progression and therapeutic response.

title: Structural Optimization and Fatigue Performance Evaluation of Balloon-Expandable Aortic Valve Stents.
authors: Tao Cai; Chaoqun Zhao; Gang Fang
abstract: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is a critical therapy for aortic stenosis, but most existing valve stents are designed for Western patients, whose aortic root anatomy differs from Chinese patients characterized by smaller annulus diameters, heavier calcification, and a higher prevalence of bicuspid valves. To address this mismatch, we designed a balloon-expandable aortic valve stent tailored for Chinese patients and systematically evaluated its performance. Four structural schemes were considered; a diamond-hexagonal composite mesh was selected based on radial strength, expansion uniformity, anchoring stability, sealing, and coronary access. Material properties of MP35N were obtained via tensile tests, and finite element models simulated crimping, recoil, and expansion. Among three end-corner geometries, the U-shaped design showed superior mechanical behavior with lower stress/strain concentrations. For stents crimped to 6.5 mm, maximum equivalent stress ranged from 1030 to 1076 MPa and plastic strain from 0.221 to 0.259; upon expansion to 20-29 mm, stress reached 1417-1493 MPa and strain 0.447-0.544, with strain concentrated at the corner ends. Simulated recoil matched experimental results within 7% relative error. Accelerated fatigue testing (4 × 108 cycles) of the bare stents revealed no fractures, displacements, or surface damage. These findings demonstrate that the optimized bare stent structure exhibits good mechanical feasibility, durability, and improved anatomical compatibility for Chinese TAVI patients, providing a promising device solution for domestic clinical application.

title: Exercise-Induced Cardiac Mechanics in Asymptomatic Primary Mitral Regurgitation: Insights from Stress Echocardiography and Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing.
authors: Markos Koukos; Yannis Dimitroglou; Dimitrios Tsartsalis; Christos Fragoulis; Charilila-Loukia Ververeli; Pagona Dritsa; Dimitrios Patsourakos; Argyro Kalompatsou; Konstantinos Tsioufis; Constantina Aggeli
journal: Hellenic journal of cardiology : HJC = Hellenike kardiologike epitheorese
abstract:
Stress echocardiography is recommended for evaluating asymptomatic primary mitral regurgitation (MR), but exercise-induced changes in myocardial mechanics and right ventricular-pulmonary artery (RV-PA) coupling remain incompletely characterized.
63 patients with moderate-to-severe or severe primary degenerative MR (NYHA I) and 20 age-matched healthy controls prospectively underwent comprehensive transthoracic and supine bicycle stress echocardiography. Left ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS), left atrial (LA) strain (reservoir, conduit and contraction), right ventricular (RV) strain, and RV-PA coupling (TAPSE/PASP) were assessed at rest and peak exercise. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) was additionally performed in a subgroup.
Compared with controls, MR patients demonstrated significantly lower exercise capacity, achieving shorter exercise duration (8.26 ± 2.32 vs. 10.32 ± 1.34 minutes, p<0.001) and lower maximal workload (78.0 ± 21.2 vs. 101.3 ± 9.9 W, p<0.001). At rest, LV GLS and RV strain were comparable between groups, whereas LA conduit and contraction strain were already altered in MR patients. Exercise unmasked lower peak GLS and impaired RV-PA coupling in the MR group, while peak LA contraction strain remained significantly different between groups. Seven patients developed exercise-induced MR deterioration, exhibiting loss of LA functional reserve with deterioration of all LA strain components, unlike patients without MR deterioration. Peak VO2 was lower in MR patients and correlated with exercise RV-PA coupling, but not with LA strain.
Exercise echocardiography combined with myocardial deformation imaging identifies chamber-specific functional abnormalities not evident at rest, providing complementary physiological insight into cardiac adaptation in asymptomatic primary MR.

title: Influence of hematocrit-dependent blood viscosity on hemodynamics of mitral paravalvular leak.
authors: Igor Szumny; Magdalena Kopernik
abstract:
Paravalvular leak (PVL) is a pathological condition that may arise following prosthetic mitral valve implantation and is characterized by regurgitant blood flow through a gap between the prosthetic valve ring and the native cardiac tissue. High-velocity flow jets generated within the leak region may produce elevated shear stresses capable of inducing mechanical damage to erythrocytes and subsequent hemolysis. The purpose of this study is to investigate the influence of blood viscosity, modulated by hematocrit variability, on flow characteristics and hemolytic potential in mitral PVL.
A computational fluid dynamics model was developed to simulate pulsatile blood flow through mitral PVL channel. The model included a time-varying left ventricular geometry, a kinematically constrained left atrium, and a simplified representation of a mechanical mitral valve with a localized paravalvular defect. Multiple physiological hematocrit levels were considered to account for viscosity variations. Non-Newtonian rheological behavior of blood was incorporated to capture shear-dependent viscosity effects.
The simulations showed a strong dependence of shear stress on hematocrit. Increasing hematocrit led to higher effective viscosity, resulting in elevated shear stress levels within the PVL jet. A near-linear relationship between hematocrit and maximum shear stress was observed, with stress values exceeding the hemolysis threshold at higher hematocrit levels. Additionally, higher hematocrit values resulted in earlier onset of critical shear stress conditions.
The results demonstrate that hematocrit significantly influences hemodynamic conditions and hemolysis risk in mitral PVL.

title: Acute deoxygenation during M-TEER: a note of caution.
authors: Michael Wester; Michael Paulus; Andreas Luchner; Christian Schach; Bernhard Unsöld; Lars S Maier; Can Martin Sag; Christine Meindl; Kurt Debl
journal: European heart journal. Imaging methods and practice
abstract:
Right-to-left (R-L) shunting through an iatrogenic atrial septal defect (iASD) after mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication. We aimed to identify factors associated with clinically relevant R-L shunting requiring emergency iASD closure.
We retrospectively analysed 444 consecutive patients undergoing successful M-TEER between 2017 and 2026. Clinical, echocardiographic, and invasive haemodynamic parameters were compared between patients requiring emergency iASD closure and the remaining cohort. Six patients (1.3%) required emergency iASD closure due to R-L shunting and acute deoxygenation. All presented with severe tricuspid regurgitation, RV dilatation, and impaired RV function. Following M-TEER, right atrial pressure exceeded left atrial pressure in five patients. Compared with controls, affected patients demonstrated reduced tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (15 ± 2 vs. 19 ± 4 mm), fractional area change (FAC) (27 ± 5% vs. 43 ± 6%), and RV free wall strain (-13 ± 2% vs. -22 ± 5%). Echocardiography underestimated invasively measured systolic pulmonary artery pressure (25.8 vs. 40.3 mmHg; P = 0.035). Oxygen saturation decreased by 3-8%, with one patient developing cardiogenic shock.
Severe tricuspid regurgitation, RV dysfunction, and elevated right atrial pressure may identify patients at risk for clinically relevant R-L shunting after M-TEER. Comprehensive RV assessment, including FAC and strain, combined with invasive hemodynamic evaluation, may improve risk stratification and facilitate timely iASD closure.

title: Right-left discordance of pulmonary artery wedge pressure under high positive end-expiratory pressure in acute eccentric mitral regurgitation.
authors: Hiroki Mori; Taku Omori; Shiro Nakamori; Kaoru Dohi

authors: Wei C Lau; Rakesh M Suri; George M Comas; John R Young; Hannah Walmsley-Solt; Richard J Bloomingdale

title: Managing a mavacamten non-responder in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: A case report.
authors: Smita Scholtz; Felix Langkamp; Volker Rudolph; Jan Michael Federspiel; Vasco Sequeira
abstract:
We report the case of a woman in her 40s with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy who remained symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy. A prior attempt of alcohol septal ablation was not performed due to unsuitable septal branch anatomy. Echocardiography demonstrated severe left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve (MV), and moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation. Biomarkers indicated significant hemodynamic stress, and magnetic resonance imaging revealed myocardial fibrosis. Treatment with the cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten was initiated and despite stepwise escalation to 15 mg/day, LVOT gradients and symptoms persisted, classifying her as a treatment non-responder. Genetic testing detected a MYH7 variant of uncertain significance, potentially associated with reduced drug effectiveness. Given refractory obstruction, the multidisciplinary heart team recommended surgical septal myectomy. Intraoperative inspection of the mitral valve revealed not only SAM-related mitral regurgitation, but degenerative MV pathology requiring MV replacement. Postoperatively, LVOT obstruction resolved, and the patient became asymptomatic.
This case underscores the clinical importance of recognition of non-response to mavacamten therapy. It highlights the need for careful evaluation of concomitant mitral valve pathology, which may significantly contribute to persistent symptoms beside left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. In selected patients, timely consideration of surgical intervention remains essential to achieve optimal hemodynamic improvement and symptomatic relief when pharmacological treatment alone is insufficient.

title: Prognostic Impact of Moderate Secondary Mitral Regurgitation After Optimized Medical Therapy in Heart Failure.
authors: Cristina Ferrero; Pau Codina; Josep Lupón; María Ruiz-Cueto; Elisabet Zamora; Andrea Borrellas; Cinta Llibre; Clara Badia-Molins; Andrea Carrete; Evelyn Santiago-Vacas; Mar Domingo; Javier Santesmases; Elena Ferrer-Sistach; Claudia Escabia; Julio Núñez; Stefan D Anker; Marco Metra; Javed Butler; Gregg W Stone; Victoria Delgado; Antoni Bayes-Genis
abstract:
The prognostic significance of moderate secondary mitral regurgitation (MR) after optimized guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in heart failure (HF) remains uncertain.
We analyzed 2,468 ambulatory HF patients with paired transthoracic echocardiography at baseline and after 12 months of optimized GDMT. The primary composite was all-cause death or first heart failure hospitalization (HFH). Secondary endpoints included all-cause mortality and recurrent HFHs.
Mean age was 66.2 ± 12.5 years, 70.6% were male, and mean baseline LVEF was 36.1% ± 13.6%. At 12 months, 80.5% of patients had no/mild MR, 15.6% had moderate MR, and 3.9% had severe MR. During a median 6.9-year follow-up, 1,240 patients experienced the primary endpoint. Compared with no/mild MR, both moderate and severe MR at 12 months were independently associated with a higher risk of the primary composite endpoint (moderate: hazard ratio [HR] 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.47-1.95; severe: HR 1.81, 95% CI 1.44-2.29; both p<0.001). Moderate MR was also independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.32-1.79; p<0.001) and recurrent HFHs (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 2.17, 95% CI 1.81-2.60). HFH rates were 9.03, 20.0, and 26.1 per 100 person-years in patients with no/mild, moderate, and severe MR, respectively. Among patients with moderate MR at 12 months, outcomes did not differ according to baseline MR severity.
In this large-scale study, residual moderate secondary MR after 12 months of optimized GDMT was common and was independently associated with increased long-term mortality and HFHs.

title: Effect of mitral valve repair on outcomes in dogs with preclinical myxomatous mitral valve disease: a retrospective cohort study.
authors: E Takahashi; S Shimizu; M Kaneko; A Takahashi; Y Nii; M Mizuno; K Kurogochi; T Sawada; T Mizukoshi; J Takeuchi; T Moriyama; N Chiba; T Mori; S Uchida; M Uechi
journal: Journal of veterinary cardiology : the official journal of the European Society of Veterinary Cardiology
abstract:
Mitral valve repair (MVR) for myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) in dogs has favorable results, but its effectiveness compared with medical treatment in preclinical (stage B2) dogs remains unclear. This study investigated whether MVR improves survival in preclinical dogs with MMVD.
Dogs diagnosed with stage B2 MMVD between October 2016 and September 2020 were divided into an MVR group and a control group receiving medical treatment. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality and the first onset of pulmonary edema. The waiting period between diagnosis and surgery in the MVR group was adjusted as a time-dependent exposure, and survival analysis was performed.
Overall, 91 and 171 dogs were enrolled in the MVR and control groups, respectively. The median observation period was 599.5 days (lower and upper quartiles: 374.0-1001.5). The primary outcome occurred in 10 dogs (11.0%) in the MVR group and 69 dogs (40.4%) in the control group. Cox proportional hazards analysis adjusted for time-dependent exposure yielded hazard ratios of 0.12 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.05-0.25, P < 0.001) for MVR and 2.85 (95% CI: 1.69-4.80, P < 0.001) for diuretic use.
Limitations include potential selection bias, limited survey response rate, inter-observer variability in diagnostic assessment, and a short follow-up period.
Dogs undergoing MVR had a lower risk of reaching the composite endpoint than medically managed dogs. These findings may assist veterinarians and owners in decision-making regarding MVR for stage B2 dogs.

title: Prevalence and prognostic role of left atrial reverse remodeling in patients undergoing mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair: insights from the Multicenter Echocardiographic Registry of patients undergoing mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair.
authors: Elisa Pezzola; Laura Lupi; Antonio Popolo Rubbio; Edoardo Sciatti; Cristina Giannini; Marta Barletta; Antonio De Luca; Davide Stolfo; Lisa Serafini; Alessandra Ricci; Luigi Fiocca; Matteo Mazzola; Luca Branca; Mauro Massussi; Michele Senni; Gianfranco Sinagra; Francesco Bedogni; Marco De Carlo; Marco Metra; Marianna Adamo
abstract:
Atrial enlargement is a complex maladaptive process related to pressure and volume overload. Left atrial reverse remodeling (LARR) has been described as a result of medical and interventional therapies. We sought to explore LARR prevalence and its prognostic implications following mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER).
Four-hundred and twenty-five patients from the MERIT-TEER (Multicenter Echocardiographic Registry of patients undergoing M-TEER) who received a successful procedure from 2012 to 2024 with available left atrial volume (LAV) have been analyzed. LARR was defined as a reduction in LAV of at least 15%. LARR prevalence and its association with the risk of heart failure hospitalization and all-cause mortality at 4 years' follow-up were evaluated in the overall population and according to mitral regurgitation etiology.At short-term follow-up, LARR was observed in 124 patients (29.20%). LARR was more prevalent among primary mitral regurgitation (PMR) patients compared with those with ventricular secondary (vSMR) and atrial secondary mitral regurgitation (aSMR) (37.23, 27.19, and 18.33%; P = 0.017). At long-term follow-up, the composite outcome occurred in 153 patients (36.2%). LARR was independently associated with lower risk of events in the overall population [adjusted hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.43-0.85, P = 0.005] and among vSMR patients (adjusted hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.26-0.71, P = 0.001), but not in aSMR or PMR.
LARR was observed in less than one-third of patients undergoing M-TEER (29.2%), occurring more frequently in PMR. LARR was independently associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization in the overall population and particularly in patients with vSMR.

title: Optimizing Echocardiographic Evaluation of Chronic Mitral Regurgitation: Comparison With Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging and Implications for Guideline Recommendations.
authors: K Carlos El-Tallawi; Clara Angulo; Mohammed Chamsi-Pasha; Fatima Qamar; Edward A Graviss; Dipan J Shah; William A Zoghbi
abstract:
The ASE (American Society of Echocardiography) guidelines recommend the presence of at least 4 specific criteria to confirm a diagnosis of definite severe mitral regurgitation (MR). However, the performance of these criteria, particularly when <4 are present, remains unclear.
This study aims to evaluate and optimize the ASE native MR guidelines by comparing them with quantitative cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), considered the reference standard for MR assessment.
In this prospective study, 177 patients underwent near-simultaneous CMR and transthoracic echocardiography for the assessment of MR. MR severity was classified using a 4-grade scale based on CMR-derived regurgitant volume, which was calculated as the difference between total left ventricular (LV) stroke volume and aortic forward flow. MR severity was similarly graded using the ASE algorithm, with quantification performed when necessary, by averaging the regurgitant volume from 3 methods: 1) the proximal isovelocity surface area method; 2) the biplane LV volumetric method; and 3) the mitral valve volumetric method.
The study cohort had a median age of 61.7 years, with 55% being men. Primary MR was the predominant pathology (73% of patients), with 42% having mitral valve prolapse and 25% presenting with flail leaflets. There was exact agreement between transthoracic echocardiography and CMR MR grading in 51% of cases, whereas agreement within 1 grade was observed in 89%. Patients who met any of the ASE severe MR criteria were predominantly classified as having grades 3 to 4 MR by CMR. The following ASE parameters demonstrated high specificity for identifying grade 4 MR by CMR: pulmonary vein systolic flow reversal (specificity 88%), enlarged LV with normal systolic function (specificity 85%), proximal isovelocity surface area radius ≥1.0 cm (specificity 83%), and vena contracta width ≥0.7 cm (specificity 80%). Combining color Doppler with either pulmonary vein systolic reversal or enlarged LV with normal function resulted in 91%-95% specificity for severe MR. Importantly, reliance on fewer ASE criteria reduced the need for quantification from 86% (4 criteria) to 73% (3 criteria) and 59% (2 criteria), thereby enhancing diagnostic efficiency.
Certain ASE criteria, especially when used in combination, are highly specific for diagnosing severe MR, even when <4 criteria are present. This study suggests that in many cases, the reliance on extensive quantification may be reduced, streamlining the diagnostic process and improving clinical workflow.

title: Vascular Plug Closure of Delayed Leaflet Perforation Post-TEER in Patient With Multiple Implantable Devices.
authors: Guanzhong Chen; Zhenyu Xiong; Menghui Liu; Ziwei Zhou; Jiantong Shen; Min Ye; Fengjuan Yao; Xinxue Liao; Xiaodong Zhuang
abstract:
Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is the main minimally invasive therapy for severe mitral regurgitation (MR) in patients at high surgical risk. Roughly 10% of patients develop recurrent MR within 1 year postoperatively. Postprocedural mitral anatomical distortion complicates reintervention, rendering recurrent MR management a common clinical challenge.
A 63-year-old man with multivalvular heart disease, chronic heart failure, multiple implantable devices and dialysis-dependent end-stage renal disease presented with symptomatic severe recurrent MR secondary to delayed anterior mitral leaflet perforation after TEER. Under combined fluoroscopic and 3-dimensional transesophageal echocardiographic guidance, our multidisciplinary team performed transcatheter closure of the perforation using a vascular plug. MR was markedly alleviated, heart failure symptoms resolved, and the patient recovered uneventfully before discharge.
TEER-related leaflet perforation caused severe recurrent MR. Percutaneous plug closure successfully downgraded MR to trivial, confirming the feasibility of this approach for mitral leaflet perforation.

title: Late Progressive Multivalvular Regurgitation After Heart Transplantation With Preserved Graft Function.
authors: Nicholas Fanous; Rita-Maria Abdo; Cobi Adams; James Healy; Aaron Adonopulos; Mayooran Namasivayam; Peter MacDonald; Alasdair Watson
abstract:
Late clinical decline after heart transplantation is commonly attributed to rejection, cardiac allograft vasculopathy, or ventricular dysfunction. Progressive structural valvular disease is less frequently emphasized when graft systolic function is preserved.
A 22-year-old woman underwent orthotopic heart transplantation at age 13 for familial restrictive cardiomyopathy. Nearly 10 years later, she developed progressive exertional fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, and dizziness despite preserved graft systolic function and no significant cardiac allograft vasculopathy. Serial imaging demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation, moderate to severe aortic regurgitation, and moderate to severe tricuspid regurgitation. She underwent redo sternotomy with bioprosthetic aortic and mitral valve replacement and tricuspid repair, with preserved ventricular function and clinical recovery at early follow-up.
This case highlights progressive multivalvular disease as an important valve-level cause of late clinical decline after heart transplantation.
Consider structural valvular disease in symptomatic long-term heart transplant recipients with preserved graft function.

title: Native Leaflet Interference After Transcatheter Mitral Valve-in-Ring: Snare-Assisted Valve-in-Valve-in-Ring Bailout.
authors: Andrea Mangiameli; Valentina Bernardini; Alessia Azzano; Eligio Miccichè; Davide Cao; Andrea Cascella; Elvis Brscic
abstract:
Native mitral leaflet interference is a rare cause of acute intraprosthetic regurgitation after transcatheter mitral valve-in-ring replacement (TMViR).
An 83-year-old woman with previous surgical mitral annuloplasty underwent transseptal TMViR for severe regurgitation from anterior mitral leaflet flail. After implantation of a 32-mm Myval Octapro valve, severe intraprosthetic regurgitation developed. High atrial positioning and prosthesis tilting allowed the flail anterior leaflet to overhang the ventricular valve edge and impair prosthetic leaflet coaptation. Balloon postdilation failed and increased instability. A contralateral gooseneck snare enabled controlled recrossing and deeper valve-in-valve-in-ring implantation, with complete regurgitation resolution and no left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
Native leaflet interference should be considered after TMViR when acute intraprosthetic regurgitation occurs.
Snare-assisted recrossing may provide selective bailout when marked tilt or instability prevents safe conventional recrossing.

title: Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair in Advanced Heart Failure and Ventricular Dysfunction: An Evolving Heart Team Strategy.
authors: Ahmed AlBadri; Moody Makar; James Burke; Salvotore Mannino; Jennifer Giuseffi; Rajnish Prasad; Gagandeep Joshi; Abdul Latif Bikak
abstract:
Patients with severe left ventricular (LV) dysfunction and mitral regurgitation are underrepresented in pivotal transcatheter edge-to-edge repair trials and are often ineligible for transplantation or LV assist devices, leaving limited options when guideline-directed medical therapy fails.
We describe 6 patients aged 38 to 82 years with LV ejection fraction 10% to 20% and severe (4+) to torrential (5+) mitral regurgitation, 4 patients presenting in or near cardiogenic shock requiring inotropic, vasopressor, or intra-aortic balloon pump support. All underwent transcatheter edge-to-edge repair as our multidisciplinary heart team strategy evolved.
With increasing experience, the heart team incorporated individualized pharmacologic or temporary mechanical support, preprocedural hemodynamic optimization, and anatomy-driven device selection. One patient initially referred for palliative care was subsequently reassessed and treated. This series illustrates how iterative multidisciplinary learning may expand transcatheter edge-to-edge repair candidacy in carefully selected, high-risk patients with advanced heart failure and profound ventricular dysfunction and limited therapeutic alternatives.

title: Transcatheter Valve-in-Band Implantation in a Swine Model of Failed Mitral Repair: A Technical Note and Proof of Feasibility.
authors: Julia E Katter; Jonathan Martinez Rivera; Meghan A Matlack; Daniel A Anderson; Emily K Leva; Allison M Tomasino; Henry J Tannous
abstract: Surgical mitral valve repair is the gold standard for severe primary mitral regurgitation (MR), yet when repairs fail, open reintervention carries substantial perioperative risk. Following band annuloplasty, minimally invasive options, such as transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR), remain largely unexplored due to a hypothetical concern around the lack of circumferential radial support. Although transapical transcatheter mitral valve-in-band (ViB) replacement has been reported in a single human case, we report the first controlled large-animal model of ViB. A 68 kg, 20-month-old female Yucatan mini pig underwent placement of a 28 mm mitral annuloplasty band, oversized to create MR, via clamshell sternotomy under cardiopulmonary bypass; a simulated dilated left atrium enabled transcatheter access. A 23 mm Edwards SAPIEN 3 Ultra valve was deployed within the band using the Commander delivery system under fluoroscopic guidance. The valve achieved stable fixation without embolization, paravalvular leak (PVL), or left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction with resolution of MR on echocardiography. The stable position was consistent with a contribution from the native anterior leaflet and annulus, although radial forces were not directly measured. The animal tolerated the procedure without complications. This first-in-animal study suggests the acute technical feasibility of TMVR within a mitral annuloplasty band and supports further investigation of percutaneous band modification strategies to optimize ViB outcomes.

title: Functional Mitral Regurgitation Trajectories in CRT-Treated HFrEF During Medical Therapy Optimization: Association with Reverse Remodeling.
authors: Oana Pătru; Silvia Luca; Dragoș Cozma; Bogdan Enache; Liviu Cirin; Mirela Virtosu; Maria-Laura Crăciun; Constantin-Tudor Luca; Simona Ruxanda Drăgan
abstract: Background: Functional mitral regurgitation (MR) is common in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) and may persist despite cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). Sacubitril/valsartan is associated with reverse remodeling in HFrEF, but MR dynamics in CRT-treated patients receiving sacubitril/valsartan remain insufficiently characterized. We aimed to characterize longitudinal changes in MR severity and assess their association with ventricular reverse remodeling in CRT-treated patients with HFrEF receiving sacubitril/valsartan. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included 188 patients with HFrEF previously treated with CRT who subsequently initiated sacubitril/valsartan. Clinical and echocardiographic assessments were performed at baseline and 10-14 months. The primary endpoint was MR improvement, defined a priori as a reduction of at least one MR grade. Changes in paired MR grade distribution were assessed using Bowker's test of symmetry. Associations between MR improvement and changes in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), and left atrial volume (LAV) were evaluated. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors independently associated with MR improvement. Results: MR improvement occurred in 116 patients (62%), while 72 (38%) had unchanged grades; no worsening was documented in the paired assessments. A significant shift toward lower MR grades was observed between baseline and follow-up (χ2 = 116.0, df = 5, p < 0.001). The proportion meeting the endpoint increased from 0% in baseline grade I to 51.2%, 80.0%, and 100% in grades II, III, and IV, respectively. Patients with MR improvement had greater increases in LVEF (9.0 vs. 7.0 percentage points, p = 0.006) and larger reductions in LVEDV (-45.7 vs. -28.6 mL, p = 0.004) and LAV (-20.4 vs. -4.2 mL, p < 0.001). The correlation between changes in LVEDV and MR grade was statistically significant but modest (r = 0.22, p = 0.002). Non-ischemic etiology and greater baseline LVEDV were independently associated with MR improvement, whereas baseline LVEF was not. The strong association with baseline MR grade partly reflects the endpoint's inherent dependence on initial severity. Conclusions: In patients with HFrEF treated with CRT who also received sacubitril/valsartan, lower MR grades were observed at follow-up and were associated with greater longitudinal changes in LVEF, LVEDV, and LAV. These findings describe parallel longitudinal changes in MR severity and cardiac structure within a combined device- and pharmacological-treatment setting. The observed changes cannot be disentangled from ongoing CRT-mediated remodeling, concomitant GDMT, changes in loading conditions, or other time-dependent factors and cannot be attributed specifically to sacubitril/valsartan.

title: Multimodality Imaging of Mitral Regurgitation.
authors: Angelo Squeri; Valeria Maria De Luca; Stefano Censi; Carmine Pizzi; Luca Bergamaschi; Nicole Suma; Nicola Forzati; Rita Conti
abstract: Mitral regurgitation is one of the most common valvular heart diseases and requires an accurate diagnostic approach to define its etiology, mechanism, severity, and therapeutic implications. This review analyzes the integrated role of the main cardiovascular imaging modalities in the assessment of mitral regurgitation. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) represents the first-line imaging modality, providing a dynamic assessment of valve anatomy, ventricular function, and hemodynamic consequences, whereas transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) provides complementary high-resolution anatomical characterization. Cardiac magnetic resonance provides accurate quantification of ventricular volumes, the regurgitant volume and fraction, and myocardial remodeling and is particularly useful when echocardiographic findings are inconclusive or discordant. Computed tomography, owing to its high spatial resolution, offers detailed information on the mitral apparatus, annulus, calcifications, and anatomical relationships, supporting the planning of surgical and transcatheter procedures. The integration of echocardiography, CMR, and CT enables more comprehensive risk stratification and personalized treatment selection. The review highlights how multimodality imaging is now essential for guiding the diagnostic and therapeutic pathway, improving intervention timing, the procedural choice, and the overall management of patients with mitral regurgitation.

title: Explainable machine learning and unsupervised anatomical phenotyping of mitral valve prolapse in patients with severe mitral regurgitation.
authors: Pooya Eini; Homa Serpoush; Mohammad Rezayee
abstract:
Mitral annular disjunction (MAD) is increasingly recognized in mitral valve prolapse (MVP), but its anatomical embedding within degenerative MVP remains incompletely defined. We assessed whether explainable supervised learning and unsupervised clustering could identify MAD-associated MVP phenotypes.
We analyzed a public surgical cohort of 979 patients with MVP and clinically significant mitral regurgitation. Etiology was classified as Barlow disease (BD) or fibroelastic deficiency (FED). Logistic regression, Random Forest and XGBoost were evaluated for MAD prediction using nested cross-validation with threshold optimization, and assessed for discrimination, calibration and net benefit (decision-curve analysis). XGBoost explainability was assessed using SHAP. UMAP-based clustering using anatomical and clinical variables (excluding MAD and etiology from the input) was performed, with prespecified cluster-number and stability sensitivity analyses.
Unsupervised phenotyping identified three anatomical clusters. The smallest cluster (n = 91, 9.3%) showed the highest MAD prevalence (36.3% vs. 12.0% and 15.8%), marked BD enrichment (95.6%), universal bileaflet prolapse and ≥ 4-scallop involvement, larger MV diameters and less chordal rupture; this phenotype was reproducible across UMAP settings. Supervised models showed only moderate MAD discrimination (XGBoost AUROC 0.695 ± 0.057; PR-AUC 0.314 ± 0.066), with modest calibration (Brier 0.13-0.20; slopes < 1) and limited net benefit, and were therefore interpreted as explanatory rather than diagnostic. SHAP identified BD status as the strongest contributor, followed by number of prolapsing scallops, mitral valve diameters, LV volumes and bileaflet prolapse.
Explainable and unsupervised analyses concordantly identified a MAD-enriched, BD-dominant bileaflet/multiscallop MVP phenotype, supporting the concept that MAD is embedded within broader annular-leaflet remodeling rather than being an isolated binary abnormality. These findings require prospective, multimodality, outcome-linked external validation before clinical application.

title: Outcomes of Patients Undergoing Mitral Valve Replacement After Failed Attempt at Mitral Valve Repair.
authors: Takuya Ogami; Ethan Chetkof; Johannes O Bonatti; Xander Jacquemyn; Yisi Wang; Christopher Pantelis; Irsa Hasan; Danny Chu; Francis D Ferdinand; Ibrahim Sultan
journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
abstract:
Mitral valve repair (MVr) is the ideal treatment strategy for degenerative mitral regurgitation. Mitral valve replacement (MVR) may be required if MVr is unsuccessful during the index surgery. The consequences of MVR following failed MVr during the same surgery are unclear.
Retrospective observational study.
Single institution, university affiliated.
All patients who underwent MVR from 2010 through 2024 were included. Patients with concomitant surgeries were included.
Patients were dichotomized into the intended repair (IR) or de novo replacement (DR) groups based on the intended procedure.
A total of 1,661 patients (mean age, 64 years; 57% female) underwent MVR. MVr was attempted in 133 patients (8%, IR group), and 1,528 underwent planned MVR (92%, DR group). The mean ejection fraction was 55%. Female sex (58.0% in the DR group v 48.9% in the IR group, p = 0.04), history of infective endocarditis (23.8% v 15.0%, p = 0.02), history of cerebrovascular disease (32.1% v 19.5%, p = 0.03), and prior sternotomy (32.1% v 15.8%, p < 0.001) were more prevalent in the DR group. After propensity score matching, perioperative morbidity and mortality were similar. The median cardiopulmonary bypass time and cross-clamp time were longer in the IR group (207 minutes v 134 minutes in the DR group and 163 minutes v 102 minutes in the DR group, respectively). Kaplan-Meier curve analysis showed similar 5-year survival (p = 0.91).
Postoperative outcomes were similar despite longer operative times in the IR group. Failure of initial MVr, leading to MVR, did not translate into adverse early or long-term outcomes. These findings suggest that repair may be more aggressively considered in patients with repairable anatomies.

title: Clinical and cardiovascular impact of pregnancy in women with Marfan syndrome.
authors: M Elena Soto; Miguel Santos-Aragón; Regina de la Mora-Cervantes
abstract:
Marfan syndrome (MS) is associated with mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1, an essential protein in elastic fibers. Cardiovascular damage in MS has serious complications such as aneurysms and aortic dissection (AD), which increase during pregnancy.
To evaluate the cardiovascular and clinical status of women with Marfan syndrome and pregnancy.
Retrospective study in women with MS or other connective tissue diseases (CTD) classified according to the 2010 Ghent criteria.
One hundred women were included, 35 were admitted as pediatric patients, and 65 as adults. Ten women without medical records were excluded. Forty-eight non-pregnant women and 46 pregnant women were analyzed. 20 births, 26 cesarean sections, 9 preeclampsia, and 14 miscarriages. Of the total group, 14 had con-genital heart disease, 36 had AD, 47 had aortic regurgitation, 22 had mitral valve regurgitation, 15 had tricuspid valve regurgitation, 39 had valve prolapse, 67 had surgeries, and 15 had stents. 19 died, 5 due to aneurysm rupture, 4 had AD, 3 had cardiogenic shock, 5 had septic shock, and 2 had hypovolemic shock.
Cardiovascular damage in pregnancies of women with MS or CTD is complex. The diagnosis of MS is late in some cases; it is at the time of delivery, and genetic counseling is not timely. These are areas of opportunity to impact on prevention, timely gynecological and obstetric status, and surgery.

title: The evolving role of cardiac CT: Emerging technologies and clinical impact.
authors: Seitaro Oda; Mami Iima; Masahiro Yanagawa; Tsukasa Saida; Satoru Ide; Koji Takumi; Rintaro Ito; Ryo Kurokawa; Maya Honda; Kentaro Nishioka; Akihiko Sakata; Keitaro Sofue; Daiju Ueda; Shunsuke Sugawara; Tadashi Watabe; Mariko Kawamura; Kenji Hirata; Shinji Naganawa
abstract: Cardiac computed tomography (CT) has progressed from a non-invasive test primarily used to exclude obstructive coronary artery disease into a comprehensive cardiovascular imaging platform for coronary artery disease, myocardial disease, valvular heart disease, and structural heart disease. Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is now endorsed as a first-line test in appropriately selected patients with stable chest pain or suspected chronic coronary syndromes because it can exclude obstructive disease, depict coronary atherosclerotic burden, support preventive treatment, and inform referral for invasive coronary angiography. At the same time, contemporary cardiac CT is moving beyond luminal stenosis. CT-derived fractional flow reserve and myocardial CT perfusion add a functional assessment of ischemia, whereas late iodine enhancement, CT-derived extracellular volume fraction, myocardial strain, and pericoronary fat attenuation index provide information on fibrosis, ventricular mechanics, vascular inflammation, and prognosis. Cardiac CT also has an established role in transcatheter valve therapy, left atrial appendage occlusion, and prosthetic valve assessment by providing a three-dimensional roadmap for device selection, access planning, and complication prediction. Photon-counting detector CT and artificial intelligence are further expanding the capabilities of cardiac CT through higher spatial resolution, spectral quantification, automated segmentation, quantitative plaque analysis, image reconstruction, and structured reporting. This review summarizes the evidence, technical foundations, clinical applications, and implementation challenges of contemporary cardiac CT, with an emphasis on its transition toward a decision-making platform for personalized cardiovascular care.

title: Partial heart transplantation in resource-limited settings: challenges and feasibility.
authors: Deng Siang Lee; Taufiek Konrad Rajab
abstract:
Partial heart transplantation provides living, growth-capable valve implants for paediatric recipients. The feasibility and challenges of implementing partial heart transplantation in resource-limited settings are evaluated, where the burden of valvular heart disease is greatest and paediatric valve replacement options remain severely limited.
A comprehensive search was conducted examining partial heart transplantation clinical outcomes, organ procurement logistics, immunosuppression requirements, and the infrastructure landscape for cardiac surgery in low-and middle-income countries. A feasibility framework was developed by mapping partial heart transplantation-specific requirements against existing low-and middle-income country cardiac surgical capacity.
Compared to orthotopic heart transplantation, several features of partial heart transplantation are inherently favourable for low-and middle-income country adaptation: it allows for longer graft ischaemia times, requires only tacrolimus monotherapy, and can source valves from hearts unsuitable for orthotopic heart transplantation. However, significant barriers persist, including limited organ procurement infrastructure, absence of regulatory frameworks for equitable donor-recipient matching, restricted access to therapeutic drug monitoring, and high rates of loss to follow-up.
Implementation of partial heart transplantation in resource-limited settings is feasible at established middle-income country cardiac surgery centres with transplant capability. A phased strategy leveraging international partnerships, existing infrastructure, and generic immunosuppression offers a realistic pathway to bringing this innovation to the children who need it most.

title: Left-sided surgical approach for tricuspid valve replacement in congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries with dextrocardia and situs inversus totalis: A case report.
authors: Chuanjie Yue; Tong Tan; Peng Sun; Jinhua Li; Changwei Ren; Yongqiang Lai; Hao Cui
abstract:
Congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA) is a rare congenital cardiac anomaly characterized by atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance, resulting in a physiologically corrected circulation. When ccTGA is combined with dextrocardia and situs inversus totalis, surgical management becomes particularly challenging because of the mirror-image anatomy and altered spatial orientation.
A 61-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea and was diagnosed with ccTGA accompanied by dextrocardia and situs inversus totalis. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe regurgitation of the systemic atrioventricular valve (morphological tricuspid valve) with dilation and systolic dysfunction of the systemic right ventricle. Comprehensive preoperative imaging confirmed atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance, right-sided cardiac apex, and complete visceral inversion. Tricuspid valve replacement was performed via a median sternotomy with the surgeon standing on the patient's left side to accommodate the mirror-image anatomy. Cardiopulmonary bypass was established safely after meticulous identification of the great vessels. A mechanical prosthetic valve was successfully implanted.
